props.title: The Bad Sleep Well
props.initialSlug: Corporate revenge tale exposes postwar corruption

sections.content: The Bad Sleep Well represents Akira Kurosawa's scathing critique of corporate corruption in post-war Japan, brilliantly reimagining Shakespeare's Hamlet in a modern business setting. The film's opening wedding sequence remains one of cinema's most masterfully orchestrated scenes, establishing the power dynamics and hidden agendas that drive the narrative. Like High and Low (1963) and The Castle of the Spider's Web (1957), Kurosawa uses noir elements to explore moral decay in Japanese society, but here he specifically targets the collusion between government and business that defined Japan's economic miracle.

movies.slug: Kurosawa transposes Macbeth to feudal Japan with stunning visual poetry

sections.content: The film's protagonist Koichi Nishi, played with smoldering intensity by Toshiro Mifune, shares DNA with other great cinematic avengers like Charles Bronson in Death Wish (1974) and Robert De Niro in Taxi Driver (1976). But Kurosawa complicates the revenge narrative by showing how Nishi's quest for justice corrupts him, much like Michael Corleone's transformation in The Godfather (1972). The labyrinthine plot reveals how corporate crime infects every level of society. SUBHEAD: Corporate Crime & Moral Corruption in Cinema

While The Bad Sleep Well pioneered the corporate thriller, its DNA can be seen in later classics like Wall Street (1987) and The Insider (1999). The film's influence extends to modern corporate critiques like Margin Call (2011) and The Big Short (2015). Kurosawa's technique of using architecture to symbolize power hierarchies influenced how later directors depicted corporate spaces, from Playtime (1967) to Office Space (1999).
